question: Why is `v.erase(v.begin())` a poor way to dequeue from a std::vector used as a queue?
option_a: It invalidates the capacity, so the next push always reallocates
option_b: It shifts every remaining element left, so each dequeue is O(n)
option_c: It is undefined behaviour when the vector has one element
option_d: It removes the last element instead of the first one
explanation: Erasing at the front moves all later elements one slot left: O(n) per dequeue and O(n²) for n dequeues. A circular buffer or a head index makes the front move instead.

question: A circular queue has capacity 4 and starts with head = 0. After enq 1, enq 2, enq 3, deq, deq, enq 4, enq 5, enq 6, which slot holds 6?
code: // slot of a new element = (head + count) % 4
explanation: After the two dequeues, head = 2 and count = 1 (element 3 in slot 2). 4 goes to (2+1)%4 = 3, 5 to (2+2)%4 = 0, and 6 to (2+3)%4 = 1.

question: What is the bug in this push_front of a ring-buffer deque?
option_a: (head - 1) % cap is negative when head == 0, so buf[-1] is written
option_b: grow() must run after the element is written, otherwise the new slot is lost in the copy
option_c: head must be incremented, because the front moves right
option_d: n must be decremented, because the front element is replaced
explanation: In C++ the remainder has the sign of the dividend, so (0 − 1) % cap is −1. Write (head − 1 + cap) % cap.

question: In a queue built from two stacks (push to in; pop from out, refilling out from in only when out is empty), what does a sequence of n operations cost?
option_a: O(n²), because one pop can move all n elements
option_b: O(n log n), because each element moves about log n times
option_c: O(n) in total, but only when pushes and pops strictly alternate so that out never grows large
option_d: O(n) in total, because each element moves between the stacks once
explanation: Each element is pushed to in once, moved to out once and popped once. A single pop can cost O(n), but the total over any sequence is O(n): O(1) amortized per operation, for any order of operations.

question: In multi-source BFS (for example, fire spreading from several cells), why are all sources pushed before the loop starts?
option_a: It makes the queue sorted by cell index, which BFS requires
option_b: The queue then holds cells in order of distance to the nearest source
option_c: It avoids needing a visited array at all, since a source cell can never be entered again
option_d: It lets the loop run once per source instead of once per cell
explanation: With every source at distance 0, the FIFO order processes all distance-d cells before any distance-(d+1) cell, so each cell gets its distance to the nearest source in one BFS. A visited array is still needed.

question: Sliding window maximum with k = 2 on a = [4, 2, 12, 3]. What is the deque (as values, front first) right after processing index 3?
explanation: After index 2 the deque is [12] (12 popped 2 and 4). At index 3, 12 (index 2) is still in the window [2, 3], and 3 < 12 is pushed behind it: [12, 3].

question: In the sliding-window-maximum deque, why can index i be discarded as soon as some later j has a[j] ≥ a[i]?
option_a: Because i will always leave the window before the next maximum has to be reported
option_b: Because the deque must stay sorted by index, and j has a larger index
option_c: Because every later window containing i contains j, so i is never needed
option_d: Because a[i] has already been reported as a maximum once
explanation: j is newer, so it stays in the window at least as long as i, and its value is at least as large. Any window where a[i] could be the answer has a[j] too, so i is useless forever.

question: For "shortest subarray with sum ≥ K" with negative values, a start index i is popped from the BACK of the deque when P[i] ≥ P[j]. Why?
option_a: Because a start with a larger prefix sum always produces a longer subarray for any end
option_b: Because P must be decreasing for the front check to be valid
option_c: Because i has already produced its answer and cannot improve
option_d: Because j is later and has a smaller prefix, so it beats i for every end
explanation: For any future end e, P[e] − P[j] ≥ P[e] − P[i] and e − j < e − i: j gives a larger sum and a shorter subarray. i can never be the better start. Starts popped from the front are the ones that already produced their best answer.

question: dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[i−k..i−1]) is computed with a monotonic deque over dp. What is the total time for n states?
option_a: O(n), because each index enters and leaves the deque once
option_b: O(n·k), because each state still scans the window
option_c: O(n log k), because the deque has to keep its values sorted like a balanced tree
option_d: O(k log n), because only k states are kept at a time
explanation: The window of dp indices slides right by one each step, so it is a sliding window maximum. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, giving O(n) in total instead of O(n·k).

question: Which property of std::deque does std::vector NOT have?
option_a: O(1) access to an element by index
option_b: Contiguous storage of all elements in one block
option_c: O(1) insertion at the front, without moving other elements
option_d: Random-access iterators that support it + n and it − n arithmetic in constant time
explanation: deque supports O(1) push_front and push_back and keeps references to existing elements valid when pushing at the ends. vector has O(1) indexing too, and it is the one with contiguous storage; deque is a table of blocks.

question: In this BFS, nodes are marked visited when DEQUEUED. What goes wrong?
option_a: Nothing is wrong: this is the standard BFS formulation found in most textbooks
option_b: A node can be pushed many times and its dist overwritten by a longer path
option_c: The source node is never visited, so dist stays −1 everywhere
option_d: The loop never terminates on graphs with cycles, because seen is checked too late
explanation: Until w is dequeued, every neighbour that sees it unvisited pushes it again and rewrites dist[w], possibly with a larger value. Mark nodes (and set dist) when they are enqueued, so each is pushed exactly once.
